rows.title: How much national debt is too much?
rows.standfirst: Most economic textbooks will tell you that there can be real dangers in running up a big national debt. A major concern is how the debt you add now could slow down economic growth in the future. Economists have not been able to nail down how much debt a country can safely take on. But they have tried.

rows.title: Kia recalls nearly 463,000 Telluride SUVs due to fire risk
rows.standfirst: Kia America is recalling nearly 463,000 Telluride SUVs — and urging owners to park their cars outside and away from other structures until an issue posing a fire hazard is fixed.

rows.title: Ghost jobs
rows.standfirst: Today's jobs report shows a slight rise in unemployment to 4%. And some frustrated job seekers are growing tired of applying for job after job with no replies, sometimes asking whether the listings are even real. And this isn't just vexing for applicants. It's also haunting economists when trying to figure out how much slack there is in the labor market, and whether interest rates should be raised or lowered. Today on the show: the rise of ghost jobs. Where they're happening and why.

rows.title: Homes have popped up on the National Mall, showing they can be built fast and cheap
rows.standfirst: From tiny homes to big ones built in hours, the Innovative Housing Showcase highlights ways to make housing more affordable and plentiful — at a time when many Americans struggle to buy a home.

rows.title: 'Washington Post' CEO tried to kill a story about himself. It wasn’t the first time
rows.standfirst: The Post's new CEO Will Lewis tried to stop the paper from publishing a story about allegations he faces in Britain. It wasn't the first time he's attempted to head off unwanted coverage. I know, because he tried to do that to me in December.

rows.title: Hiring jumps in May but so does unemployment
rows.standfirst: U.S. employers added 272,000 jobs in May -- more than forecasters had expected. The unemployment rate inched up to 4% from 3.9% in April.

rows.title: Black workers sue General Mills over alleged racial discrimination at a Georgia plant
rows.standfirst: The eight employees say that since the plant opened in 1988, many systems in place have benefited white workers more than Black staff. They claim that HR has ignored “egregious incidents of racism.”

rows.title: Elon Musk's giant Starship rocket rumbles into space once more
rows.standfirst: This is the fourth test for Starship, and this time, it returned successfully to earth.

rows.title: Why California's high speed rail was always going to blow out
rows.standfirst: 99.5 percent of megaprojects are either over time, over budget or have lower benefits than expected. What's going wrong? Today, we look at case studies from California's high speed rail project to the Sydney Opera House to consider the do's and don'ts of ambitious projects.

rows.title: Stock traders are trying to beat the market — by copying lawmakers
rows.standfirst: The law requiring lawmakers to disclose their stock trades spurred an unintended consequence: a cottage industry with funds modeled on lawmakers' investments. These funds are beating the market.

rows.title: This is what Russian propaganda looks like in 2024
rows.standfirst: The hallmarks of Russian-back influence are consistent: trying to erode support for Ukraine, discrediting democratic institutions and seizing on existing political divides.

rows.title: Why the U.S. helps pay for Israel's military
rows.standfirst: The United States has been a supporter of Israel since the nation's establishment in 1948. With the civilian death toll rising in the Israel-Hamas war, growing scrutiny is mounting over just how much the U.S. should support Israel's military. Today, a historical explanation for why the United States tied itself so closely to support for Israel.

rows.title: The history of light (classic)
rows.standfirst: For thousands of years, getting light was a huge hassle. You had to make candles from scratch. This is not as romantic as it sounds. You had to get a cow, raise the cow, feed the cow, kill the cow, get the fat out of the cow, cook the fat, dip wicks into the fat. All that--for not very much light. Now, if we want to light a whole room, we just flip a switch.

rows.title: The NAACP calls on American Airlines to investigate recent discrimination incidents
rows.standfirst: Derrick Johnson, president of the NAACP, says that without an appropriate response from American Airlines, the civil rights organization will be forced to reinstate an advisory against the airline.

rows.title: Common economic myths, debunked
rows.standfirst: Maybe you've heard these things on social media, in the news, and take them as fact: More than half of the adults in the US live paycheck to paycheck, the trade deficit is always bad, and making the super wealthy pay their fair share will fix everything .

rows.title: What's with all the tiny soda cans? And other grocery store mysteries, solved.
rows.standfirst: There's a behind the scenes industry that helps big brands decide questions like: How big should a bag of chips be? What's the right size for a bottle of shampoo? And yes, also: When should a company do a little shrinkflation?

rows.title: Oil gluts, Russian bucks, and Starbucks
rows.standfirst: Indicators of the Week is back! This week, we've got indicators about oil gluts, big bucks for Ukraine and fewer bucks at Starbucks. (Apologies for the slurping.)

rows.title: Elon Musk wins back his $44.9 billion Tesla pay package in shareholder vote
rows.standfirst: Tesla shareholders voted to restore Musk's record pay package that was thrown out by a Delaware judge earlier this year. A separate vote approved moving the company’s legal home to Texas.

rows.title: Is Google search getting worse?
rows.standfirst: There are many anecdotal complaints about Google search not being what it used to be. A German computer scientist and his colleagues put this theory to the test recently focusing on product reviews. Today on the show, we bring their findings to Google's chief search scientist.

rows.title: You can get your passport renewed online again. Here's how it works
rows.standfirst: The rollout of online passport renewal is restricted to certain windows, beginning midday Eastern time weekly. Officials say the processing times for renewing online are the same as renewing by mail.

rows.title: X now hides your 'likes' from other users, whether you like it or not
rows.standfirst: The platform X is now hiding all users' likes, with few exceptions. It says the change protects users' privacy — but critics say it removes a layer of accountability in the process.

rows.title: Supreme Court rejects challenge to abortion pill accessibility
rows.standfirst: The court said that the challengers, a group called the Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, had no right to be in court at all since neither the organization nor its members could show they had suffered any concrete injury.

rows.title: A jury says Chiquita should pay millions over paramilitary killings in Colombia
rows.standfirst: The jury awarded plaintiffs $38.3 million in damages saying that Chiquita was liable for killings perpetrated by the AUC–Autodefensas Unidas de Colombia (the United Self-Defense Forces of Colombia).

rows.title: While women outnumber men on campus, their later earnings remain stuck
rows.standfirst: On college campuses, women are making inroads in male-dominated fields like engineering and business. But that is not eliminating the earnings gaps in leadership and income in the workplace.

rows.title: Bringing a tariff to a graphite fight
rows.standfirst: Graphite is sort of the one-hit wonder of minerals. And that hit? Pencils. Everyone loves to talk about pencils when it comes to graphite. If graphite were to perform a concert, they'd close out the show with "pencils," and everyone would clap and cheer. But true fans of graphite would be shouting out "batteries!" Because graphite is a key ingredient in another important thing that we all use in our everyday lives: lithium ion batteries.

rows.title: Has the Fed lost the dot plot?
rows.standfirst: The Federal Reserve introduced a visual tool called the "dot plot" in 2012 to communicate where officials think interest rates should be in the coming years. The dot plot is eagerly dissected by Fed watchers looking for insight on future policy, but others think that the dot plot has become a visual example of just how little the Fed can predict where the economy is going.

rows.title: The Fed holds rates steady, sees only one rate cut in 2024 as inflation cools slowly
rows.standfirst: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady while signaling it can cut rates only once this year. The decision came after data earlier showed inflation cooling slightly.

rows.title: Hot dog-eating champ Joey Chestnut won't compete this July 4. What's the beef?
rows.standfirst: The 16-time reigning champion lost his spot in this year's competition after signing an endorsement deal with a company that makes plant-based hot dogs, potentially clearing the way for an underdog.

rows.title: Biden administration announces a plan for removing medical debt from credit reports
rows.standfirst: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau released proposed federal regulations that would prevent unpaid medical bills from being counted on consumers’ credit reports.

rows.title: This prison newspaper has been publishing for more than a century
rows.standfirst: A newspaper in a Minnesota prison began publishing more than a century ago. The paper covers prison life and gives its writers purpose. It’s one of around two dozen similar publications nationwide.

rows.title: The Vapes of Wrath
rows.standfirst: When the vape brand Juul first hit the market back in 2015, e-cigarettes were in a kind of regulatory limbo. At the time, the rules that governed tobacco cigarettes did not explicitly apply to e-cigarettes. Then Juul blew up, fueled a public health crisis over teen vaping, and inspired a regulatory crackdown. But when the government finally stepped in to solve the problem of youth vaping, it may have actually made things worse.

rows.title: Boeing's woes, Bilt jilts, and the Indicator's stock rally
rows.standfirst: Indicators of the Week are back! We are here, as always, to bring you the most fascinating snapshots from the week of economic news.

rows.title: After uproar over ethics, new 'Washington Post' editor won't take the job
rows.standfirst: Washington Post Chief Executive and Publisher Will Lewis' pick to be its lead editor has withdrawn from the job. Robert Winnett of the U.K.'s Telegraph was scheduled to start after the U.S. elections.

rows.title: American Airlines CEO aims to 'rebuild trust' after Black men removed from flight
rows.standfirst: CEO Robert Isom vows immediate action following the incident involving eight Black men on a flight from Phoenix to JFK, as well as other alleged accounts of racial discrimination toward passengers.

rows.title: A captive market: The high price of prison phone calls
rows.standfirst: When Diane Lewis' son, Jovaan, was sentenced to prison, she told him to call her every day. What he didn't know at the time is that those collect calls often meant Diane was unable to pay her other bills. Today on the show, how prison phone calls got so expensive, and the movement to make them free.

rows.title: The Supreme Court leaves a Trump-era offshore tax in place on investors
rows.standfirst: The case had potentially trillions of dollars in tax consequences for the federal budget, and the court's decision could have severely limited congressional options in enacting tax policy.

rows.title: To help the economy, an Alabama county is betting on home-based child care
rows.standfirst: A project in Alabama seeks to drastically grow the number of home-based child care options. It could help the state's workforce, especially during nontraditional hours.

rows.title: U.S. home prices have far outpaced paychecks. See what it looks like where you live
rows.standfirst: In nearly half of metro areas, buyers must make more than $100,000 to afford a median-priced home, a Harvard University report finds. And home prices this year reached a new all-time high.

rows.title: A supermarket trip may soon look different, thanks to electronic shelf labels
rows.standfirst: With electronic shelf labels, prices can change up to six times a minute. Grocers including Walmart, Whole Foods and Schnucks are adopting them.

rows.title: Why is everyone talking about Musk's money?
rows.standfirst: We've lived amongst Elon Musk headlines for so long now that it's easy to forget just how much he sounds like a sci-fi character. He runs a space company and wants to colonize mars. He also runs a company that just implanted a computer chip into a human brain. And he believes there's a pretty high probability everything is a simulation and we are living inside of it.

rows.title: Ralph Lauren unveils Team USA's Olympic and Paralympic uniforms
rows.standfirst: The opening ceremony outfits feature jeans paired with a navy blue blazer trimmed in white and red. The closing ceremony features a white moto-style jacket accompanied with white jeans.

rows.title: Invest like a Congress member
rows.standfirst: There are some new funds that track stock trading by members of Congress and their family. So we thought, why don't we get in on that? Today on the show, we crack open the Planet Money Investment Jar to learn more about how our political leaders play the market, investing in funds tracking Democratic and Republican stock trades.

rows.title: Amazon's struggling union joins forces with the Teamsters
rows.standfirst: For two years, Amazon has refused to recognize its single unionized warehouse, organized by the upstart Amazon Labor Union. Now the hefty Teamsters is lending its muscle to the union effort.

rows.title: If AI is so good, why are there still so many jobs for translators?
rows.standfirst: Machine translation of foreign languages has been good for a while. And yet human translators are still in demand. Why isn’t AI killing these jobs? And even if it isn’t, how is it reshaping them?

rows.title: A year after the Titan submersible implosion, investigators still don't have answers
rows.standfirst: OceanGate's Titan submersible imploded on its way to the Titanic wreck one year ago. The Coast Guard initially had 12 months to complete its investigation, but says it needs more time.

rows.title: Do immigrants really take jobs and lower wages?
rows.standfirst: We wade into the heated debate over immigrants' impact on the labor market. When the number of workers in a city increases, does that take away jobs from the people who already live and work there? Does a surge of immigration hurt their wages?

rows.title: Indicators of the Week: Debate Edition
rows.standfirst: Indicators of the Week is BACK! This week we're doing something just a little bit different. You see, it's the same 'ol Indicators of the Week you're used to, but as a nod to last night's presidential debate, this time, it's debate style.

rows.title: Tractor Supply slashes its DEI and climate goals after a right-wing pressure campaign
rows.standfirst: The rural lifestyle retailer, with stores in 49 states, says it will withdraw its carbon emissions goals, cut its DEI roles and stop sponsoring Pride events after an online outcry from conservatives.

rows.title: Supreme Court just made it harder for federal agencies to regulate in sweeping ruling
rows.standfirst: The decision overturned Chevron v. The Natural Resources Defense Council, a 1984 decision that was not particularly controversial when it was announced 40 years ago.

rows.title: A watchdog group targets payday lenders with a ‘2 strikes’ rule to help borrowers
rows.standfirst: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau is set to move ahead with a long-stalled rule to protect borrowers from repeated attempts to collect loan payments from bank accounts with insufficient funds.

rows.title: Jury orders NFL to pay billions in 'Sunday Ticket' case for violating antitrust laws
rows.standfirst: The lawsuit covered 2.4 million residential subscribers and 48,000 businesses in the United States who paid for the package of out-of-market games from the 2011 through 2022 seasons on DirecTV.

rows.title: Do polluters pay, or do they get paid?
rows.standfirst: For years, rich nations have sent money to lower-income countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change. But it turns out, these wealthy nations are finding creative ways to funnel some of that financing back into their own economies. Today, we look at how the climate crisis is reviving a debate over how money should flow from rich to less-rich nations.

rows.title: The race is on to build EV battery-recycling plants in the U.S.
rows.standfirst: Federal spending is turbocharging a scramble to build more EV battery-recycling plants in the U.S. and make them more efficient and eco-friendly too.

rows.title: Supreme Court limits SEC's powers to impose fines
rows.standfirst: The U.S. Supreme Court declared unconstitutional the way the Securities and Exchange Commission imposes fines for fraudulent conduct and requires that wrongdoers give back their ill-gotten gains.

rows.title: At the factory that builds the 737 Max, Boeing rethinks how it trains new hires
rows.standfirst: Troubled plane maker Boeing is changing how it trains new recruits at the factory near Seattle where it assembles the 737 Max, part of a broader effort to improve quality after a midair blowout.

rows.title: Amazon becomes the 5th U.S. company to reach $2 trillion in stock market value
rows.standfirst: Amazon's stock has gained 52% in the past 12 months, partly driven by enthusiasm for the company's investments in artificial intelligence.

rows.title: What's going to happen to the Trump tax cuts?
rows.standfirst: The last major overhaul of the tax code was in 2017, when Republicans passed the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act. Much of that is set to expire next year, and that means a big debate over tax policy is looming.

rows.title: Planet Money
rows.standfirst: Money makes the world go around, faster and faster all the time. At Planet Money, a multimedia team of reporters tracks down the economists, investors and regular folks who are trying to make sense of the rapidly changing global economy.

rows.title: The Carriage Tax (Update)
rows.standfirst: (Note: A version of this episode originally ran in 2019.)

rows.title: These nurse managers were burnt out. Then their hospital gave them a 4-day workweek
rows.standfirst: Since the pandemic, hospitals have seen soaring turnover among clinical managers who oversee teams of nurses. Now some hospitals, including AtlantiCare in New Jersey, have introduced a four-day workweek.
